canonical_statement: The study aimed to determine the prevalence and patient-level risk factors of clinically significant pediatric drug-drug interaction exposures in hospitalized children.
The study aimed to determine variation in clinically significant DDI prescribing across US children's hospitals.
The investigators conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study using the Pediatric Health Information System (PHIS).
PHIS included billing and medication-use data from 52 tertiary care children's hospitals affiliated with the Children's Hospital Association.
Eligible encounters were inpatient or observation hospitalizations of patients younger than 26 years discharged from a PHIS hospital between Jan 1, 2016 and Dec 31, 2018.

canonical_statement: Clinically significant DDIs were defined using a published pediatric expert-consensus list of 53 medication pairings selected for safety relevance.
A patient was considered exposed to a DDI pair when both medications were administered on at least 1 hospital day during the same hospitalization.

outcome.definition: Both medications in a specified DDI pair administered on the same hospital day

canonical_statement: Topical, ophthalmic, and otic medication routes were excluded from DDI exposure ascertainment.
When a DDI pairing represented a drug class or pharmacologic mechanism, exposure was assessed across drugs in that class or mechanism, with source-specific exclusions.
DDIs were further classified with Lexicomp interaction risk grades, including C (monitor therapy), D (modify regimen), and X (avoid combination) among the studied pairs.
DDI effects were categorized as increased serum concentration, decreased serum concentration, increased risk of adverse drug events, altered drug metabolism, or multiple effects.
Unadjusted hospital DDI proportions were calculated as hospitalizations with at least one DDI exposure divided by total hospitalizations.
DDI exposure rates were calculated as hospital days with DDI exposure divided by total hospital days and expressed per 1000 hospital days.
Adjusted hospital-level DDI exposure proportions were estimated with a generalized linear mixed-effects model including hospital as a random effect.
The adjusted hospital-level model included age, sex, race and ethnicity, payer, number of complex chronic conditions, length of stay, service line, geographic region, ICU status, and case mix index.
Patient-level factors independently associated with clinically significant DDI exposure were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression.
Analyses were performed in SAS version 9.4 and used P < .05 as the statistical significance threshold.
The Vanderbilt University Medical Center IRB determined that analysis of the deidentified PHIS data did not constitute human subjects research (IRB 160244).

Any clinically significant DDI occurred in 47,414 hospitalizations (2.03%), accounting for 328,585 DDI-exposure patient-days; the exposure rate was 34.91 per 1000 hospital days and 370.72 per 1000 days among DDI-exposed patients.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that clinically significant DDI exposure is substantial in hospitalized children and is concentrated among older patients, patients with more complex chronic conditions, longer stays, and surgical service-line diagnoses.

The authors emphasized that roughly one-quarter of DDI-exposed hospitalizations involved a contraindicated risk-grade X pairing and that higher-risk pairings were used for longer durations than lower-risk pairings.

The authors interpreted the wide between-hospital variation in DDI prescribing as evidence that some exposures may be unwarranted and preventable, while acknowledging that some prescribing is unavoidable because of case mix and clinical necessity.
The authors argued that risk grade may be more clinically useful in children than generic severity classifications because it incorporates interaction relevance, evidence, and iatrogenic risk.
The authors proposed prioritizing pediatric-specific clinically significant DDI combinations in medication-alert systems rather than treating all database-flagged interactions equivalently.

The authors proposed targeting DDI decision-support interventions toward patients and providers involved in frequent DDI exposures rather than applying equal-intensity interventions to all hospitalized children.
The authors proposed incorporating patient-specific complexity, laboratory values, and illness severity into customized DDI alerts to better communicate risk.
The authors concluded that further studies are needed to quantify adverse events caused by pediatric DDI exposures and to identify modifiable factors for safer medication use.

The article's final conclusion was that approximately 2% of patients treated at US children's hospitals were prescribed clinically significant DDI combinations and that large hospital variation represents an opportunity for medication-safety improvement.
The retrospective study design limited the available clinical detail and causal interpretation.
PHIS contained incomplete patient-level clinical information for interpreting the clinical context of DDI exposures.
Because PHIS includes children's hospitals, results may not generalize to community hospitals.
Exclusion of normal newborns, NICU patients, and peri- or postpartum obstetrical care limited generalizability to those populations.
The study evaluated only 53 predefined clinically significant DDI pairings and may therefore have underestimated the total frequency of clinically significant DDI exposure.
The study did not measure the rate or severity of adverse drug events resulting from the identified DDI exposures.
Unmeasured differences in hospital specialization or case mix could contribute to observed between-hospital variation despite statistical adjustment.
